title: Programming Paradigms
overview: A programming paradigm is a general style of solving/programming a problem. Cambridge requires low-level, imperative/procedural, object-oriented and declarative approaches. At A2 you should be able to reason about addressing modes, modular procedural code, class relationships and declarative facts/rules/goals.
syllabusPoints: Explain the idea of a programming paradigm.
Use low-level concepts including immediate, direct, indirect, indexed and relative addressing.
Use imperative/procedural programming concepts and routines.
Use OOP concepts including classes, objects, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism and aggregation/containment.
Use declarative facts, rules and goals.

definitions.definition: A broad approach/style for representing computation and organising programs.
Programs expressed as commands that update state in a defined control flow.
Controlling access to an object's internal state through a public interface.
A class deriving attributes/methods from another class; an is-a relationship.
The same method/interface producing class-specific behaviour.
A has-a relationship where an object contains/references objects of another class.
Specifying facts/rules or a desired relationship rather than an explicit step-by-step algorithm.

sections.title: Low-level programming and addressing
content: Immediate addressing places a literal value in the instruction. Direct addressing gives the memory address of the operand. Indirect addressing points to a location that contains the operand address. Indexed addressing combines a base address with an index. Relative addressing forms an address relative to a reference such as the program counter.

sections.title: Imperative/procedural programming
content: Variables hold state, and sequence, selection and iteration determine control flow. Procedures/functions decompose the solution, use parameters and local variables, and improve reuse/testing.

sections.title: Classes and objects
content: A class is a blueprint containing attributes and methods; an object/instance has its own state. Private attributes protect invariants, while getters/setters or other public methods provide controlled interaction.

examples.label: Cambridge-style pseudocode
examples.content:
CLASS BankAccount
  PRIVATE Balance : REAL
  PUBLIC PROCEDURE Deposit(Amount : REAL)
    Balance <- Balance + Amount
  ENDPROCEDURE
ENDCLASS

sections.title: Inheritance, polymorphism, aggregation
content: Inheritance models is-a and can reuse/extend behaviour. Polymorphism allows a common method call to behave differently for subclasses. Aggregation/containment models has-a—for example a Team object contains Player objects. Use the relationship that matches the real model rather than forcing inheritance.

sections.title: Declarative programming
content: Facts record known relationships, rules derive new relationships and goals/queries ask what can be proven. The language/runtime chooses the search/evaluation steps rather than the programmer explicitly controlling each step.

sections.title: Choosing a paradigm
content: Low-level code gives hardware control but low portability. Procedural code suits clear algorithms. OOP suits systems with interacting entities/state and reuse. Declarative approaches suit relation/rule-based problems. Real applications can combine paradigms.

examTips: Encapsulation is controlled access to internal state, not merely 'putting code in a class'.
For addressing modes, say where the actual operand/value is obtained.
commonMistakes: Saying declarative programming has no logic.
